n: Account Takeover and Money Mule Account Networks (Cyber Angle)
ds: Criminals take over legitimate accounts through phishing, malware, credential stuffing and SIM swaps, or recruit and trick people into acting as money mules, in order to receive and move proceeds of cyber-enabled fraud. Networks of mule accounts layer funds quickly to cash-out channels, often across institutions.

src.t: FinCEN, Advisory to Financial Institutions on Cyber-Events and Cyber-Enabled Crime (FIN-2016-A005, 2016)
FATF, Illicit Financial Flows from Cyber-Enabled Fraud (2023)
Europol, European Money Mule Action (EMMA) press releases (annual editions, e.g. EMMA 9, 2023)

cn.rt: Takeover and mule accounts moving scam proceeds; loan and card takeover enables cash-out, and call centre used for social engineering and credential resets.

rat: Account takeover and mule accounts moving scam proceeds quickly to cash-out.

ind.n: Credential, device or contact detail change followed by payments
ind.cx: Password, email or phone change then new payee and payment in the same session or day.
ind.ds: Password, email or phone details are changed, followed in the same session or day by a new payee and large outbound payments.
ind.cn: Credential or contact change followed by new payee and payments

ind.n: Login from new device with remote-access tooling
ind.cx: Session uses remote-desktop or screen-sharing applications at payment time.
ind.ds: Remote-desktop, screen-sharing, emulator or scripted-control tools are detected during onboarding, login or payment sessions.
ind.cn: Remote-access, emulator or automation tools in session

ind.n: Many failed logins across accounts from one source
ind.cx: Credential stuffing pattern with later successful access.
ind.ds: Repeated failed authentication attempts, often across accounts from one source, followed by successful access.
ind.cn: Multiple failed logins followed by success

ind.n: Inbound funds quickly forwarded out in near-equal amounts
ind.cx: Pass-through behaviour with minimal retained balance.
ind.ds: Funds received into an account are forwarded onward within a very short period, often in near-equal amounts and leaving minimal balance.

ind.n: Recently opened account receiving payments from multiple unrelated victims
ind.cx: New account collects scam receipts from varied sources.
ind.ds: A new or low-activity account receives payments from several unrelated individuals who appear to be victims of fraud or phishing, followed by onward movement or cash-out.
ind.cn: Account receiving funds from multiple apparent fraud victims

ind.cx: Student, pensioner or unemployed customer processes large flows.
ind.ds: Turnover or volumes materially exceed what the customer's declared occupation, income, age or circumstances would support.
ind.cn: Account activity inconsistent with declared occupation or income

ind.n: Payments to crypto exchanges or cash-out channels soon after receipt
ind.cx: Funds sent to exchanges, gift-card merchants or remittance providers immediately.
ind.ds: Funds sent to exchanges, gift-card merchants or remittance providers immediately.

ind.n: Same beneficiary reached by many mule accounts
ind.cx: Graph shows many accounts paying the same ultimate beneficiary.
ind.ds: Graph shows many accounts paying the same ultimate beneficiary.

ind.n: Payee name verification fails or mismatches
ind.cx: Names mismatch or accounts recently created for the payee.
ind.ds: Names mismatch or accounts recently created for the payee.

ind.n: Customer recruited online for fake job offering payment handling
ind.cx: Customer describes job ads asking to receive and forward funds.
ind.ds: Customer describes job ads asking to receive and forward funds.

ctl.ds: Analyses typing, navigation, remote-access tooling, call-in-progress signals and deviation from baseline to spot coached, scripted or hijacked sessions. It detects coercion and takeover.
Requires phishing-resistant authentication and additional verification on risky sessions, credential or payee changes and large payments. It blocks unauthorised access and payments.
Rules that alert on abnormal count, value or speed of movements over defined windows compared with customer profile and peer norms. They provide baseline coverage across many typologies.

ctl.n: Dynamic payment friction and scam warnings
ctl.ds: Risk-scored payments trigger a purpose question and a tailored scam warning, or a call-back, before release to the customer. It gives the customer a chance to reconsider and interrupts payments made under deception.

Matches accounts, devices, identifiers and beneficiaries against industry fraud sharing and ingests law-enforcement, commercial and open-source threat feeds, including victim reports from other institutions. It catches known bad actors early.

Detects use of VPN, proxy and anonymising services and compares access geolocation with declared residence and sanctioned or high-risk jurisdictions. It reveals concealed location and supports geographic restrictions.
Links accounts, devices, addresses, directors and beneficiaries to surface rings, shared attributes and flow structures that single-account views miss. It supports detection of organised networks.
Model that scores inbound-then-outbound pass-through, new-payee churn, counterparty diversity and profile mismatch to flag likely mule accounts. It prioritises accounts for review and restriction.

ctl.n: Specialist investigation and suspicious activity reporting
ctl.ds: Trained analysts investigate alerts with typology playbooks, document rationale and file reports where suspicion is formed, with prompt reporting to the competent authority. It converts alerts into actionable intelligence.

Applies additional information gathering, corroboration, monitoring and senior review to relationships or transactions assessed as higher risk, covering purpose, expected activity, ownership and funds. The depth is proportionate to the risk drivers identified.
Traces exposure of deposit and withdrawal addresses to illicit clusters and screens wallets with risk-scored alerts. It reveals on-chain exposure.

Checks the payee name against the destination account before release and warns on no-match or close-match, and flags payee-name mismatches against contracted entities. It interrupts misdirected, spoofed and fraudulent payments.

Briefs front-line, onboarding and investigation staff on current red flags, typologies and escalation routes, including sector-specific patterns and professional-enabler behaviours. It improves recognition of suspicious activity that rules alone cannot see.
